summary:
Global SAR is an interactive 3D globe that turns real NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data into evidence anyone can read. Radar sees through clouds, smoke and darkness, but its images look like grey noise to most people and sit in large HDF5 files behind logins. Global SAR closes that gap: select an earthquake, flood, wildfire, volcano or deforestation event, swipe between before and after radar images, read a Simple or Scientific explanation in real units (cm, dB, km²), and ask a built-in assistant about what you see.

We built five investigations on genuine NISAR L-band data: about 45 cm of ground motion from the June 2026 Venezuela earthquakes, 322-379 km² of new flood water in Mozambique, 35.7 km² of cleared Amazon forest, 68 km² of burned canopy in Colorado and an 11-date volcano time series. A live coverage probe lists the real NISAR passes over any point on Earth. Every layer records its product, track, frame, dates and processing steps, and nothing is simulated. The goal: a first-time user can say what changed within one minute, with no radar background.
details:
Global SAR – Exploring Changes on Earth with Radar

What is Global SAR?

Global SAR is a web platform that lets people explore changes happening on Earth's surface using satellite radar data. We built it around NASA and ISRO's NISAR mission because we wanted to make radar imagery easier to understand and more useful to people who are not familiar with remote sensing.

The platform has an interactive 3D globe where users can select an investigation, look at satellite images from different dates, and compare what changed. They can swipe between images, view them side by side, or use an overlay. Each investigation also includes a timeline and two levels of explanation: a simpler overview and a more scientific breakdown.

We did not want users to just look at satellite images without knowing what they were seeing. That is why we included measurement units, map markers, explanations, and information about how each result was produced.

What Have We Found?

We processed real NISAR data and used it to investigate five different events:

  • Venezuela Earthquakes – June 24, 2026: We used GUNW interferometry data to examine ground movement. Our analysis showed line-of-sight displacement reaching approximately 45 cm along parts of the coast. We also checked a pre-event image pair, which had a noise floor of around 3.5 cm.
  • Limpopo Floods, Mozambique – January 2026: Using GCOV backscatter data, we mapped newly inundated areas around Chókwè. Depending on the speckle filter used, our estimates ranged from 322 to 379 km².
  • União do Sul, Brazil – October 2026: We examined changes in HV polarization to identify forest canopy loss. Our analysis detected approximately 35.7 km² of strong loss. We also compared the results with INPE DETER alerts.
  • Aspen Acres Fire, Colorado – June 2026: We used HV backscatter changes to investigate the effects of the fire and identified approximately 68 km² of woody canopy loss.
  • Krasheninnikov Volcano – 2026: We brought together 11 acquisition dates to create a backscatter time series, allowing users to follow changes over time using a consistent image stretch.

These figures come from our own processing and analysis of the available satellite products. They should be understood in that context, rather than as official measurements published by NASA.

How Does It Work?

We built a processing pipeline using Node.js and Python.

The first stage uses Node.js to retrieve NASA ASF browse images and match them with their geographic footprints. This makes it possible to display the imagery in the correct location on the globe.

The second stage uses Python to process the actual scientific data. With an Earthdata token, our scripts access the required HDF5 data and calculate the layers used in the investigations.

For ground movement, we use interferometric phase measurements and the relationship between phase change and line-of-sight displacement:

(d=-\frac{\phi\lambda}{4\pi})

We also apply ionospheric correction and coherence masking to reduce unreliable measurements.

For flood detection, we compare radar backscatter values and use histogram-based thresholds to identify areas that have become inundated.

For forest loss, we analyse changes in HV polarization using a logarithmic ratio. This helps us identify areas where the radar response has changed significantly.

The processed results are packaged as static data that the website can load directly. The platform also connects to public services such as ASF Search, NASA CMR, NASA GIBS, and weather services to provide additional information.

Why Use SAR?

Optical satellite images are useful, but they have an important limitation: clouds, smoke, and darkness can make it difficult or impossible to observe the ground.

Synthetic Aperture Radar works differently. It sends and receives microwave signals, so it can collect useful observations at night and through many cloud conditions. This makes it particularly valuable when monitoring floods, fires, earthquakes, and other events where getting information quickly matters.

We wanted to make this kind of data easier to explore without requiring users to download large scientific files or learn specialised processing software first.

Making the Results Understandable

One of the main challenges was presenting scientific data without making it misleading or unnecessarily complicated.

Every investigation includes information about its source data, acquisition dates, product type, track, frame, and processing steps. We distinguish between original NASA browse imagery and layers calculated by our team.

We also show uncertainty and limitations where they matter. For example, the flood estimates are presented as a range because different speckle filters produce different results.

The platform is designed for exploration and observation. It does not predict earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, or other disasters, and we do not present our calculations as official emergency warnings.

Additional Features

We added several features to make the platform more useful beyond the five prepared investigations.

  • AI Assistant: Users can ask questions about the platform and its investigations. The assistant uses a knowledge base and the currently selected investigation to provide answers. It can explain information in English or Turkish and avoids giving unsupported answers when the available sources do not contain enough information.
  • SAR Lens: A feature for exploring recent radar observations from NISAR and Sentinel-1.
  • Event Catalogues: The platform brings together information from sources such as USGS earthquakes, NASA EONET, FIRMS fire detections, and other public event feeds.
  • Detailed Exploration: Users can zoom into areas of interest and inspect satellite imagery more closely.
  • Guided Tutorial: First-time visitors can follow a walkthrough to learn how to use the platform.
  • Accessibility and Mobile Support: We included English and Turkish language options, a lighter mode for less powerful devices, reduced-motion support, and an installable mobile web experience.

Technologies and Development

The website is built with TypeScript, React 19, MapLibre GL, and Vite. Our data-processing tools use Node.js and Python.

We also Developed And Created Agent AI Assistant For Our Project.

We developed the project with a focus on keeping it accessible. The website is hosted through GitHub Pages, and users do not need to install software, run their own server, or provide an API key to explore the platform.

We used Vitest, Python tests, and Playwright for automated testing throughout development.

What We Considered During Development

Scientific accuracy was one of our biggest priorities. We had to make sure that the data was displayed in the correct geographic location, that comparisons used appropriate acquisition dates, and that the processing methods were clearly explained.

We also considered how people with different levels of technical knowledge would use the website. Someone who has never worked with SAR data should still be able to understand the basic findings, while a more experienced user should be able to inspect the scientific details.

Finally, we wanted the platform to work on different devices and browsers without requiring specialised hardware.

Global SAR is our attempt to make real satellite radar data easier to access, explore, and understand. Instead of showing people only the final result, we wanted to let them investigate the imagery and see how we reached our conclusions.
